title: Benchmarking
concept: Benchmarking measures code performance to guide optimization decisions
why: Correctness alone isn't enough — production code must be fast. Benchmarking quantifies performance so you can compare implementations objectively. It answers: 'Is my new algorithm actually faster?' and 'Which approach should I use for this hot path?' Without benchmarks, optimization is guesswork.
theory: XIOM provides the `bench` module with `@bench` attribute functions. Benchmarks are separate from tests and run with `xiom bench`. The runner warms up the JIT/CPU caches, runs the benchmark many times, and reports mean throughput (operations/sec) with standard deviation. Benchmarks should be deterministic and not include I/O. Use `bench::black_box()` to prevent the compiler from optimizing away the code being measured.
tips: Always use `bench::black_box()` on results to prevent dead code elimination
Run benchmarks on a quiet machine for consistent results
Benchmark both your approach AND alternatives to make data-driven decisions
common_mistakes: Benchmarking I/O-bound code as if it were CPU-bound
Forgetting `black_box()` — the compiler may optimize away the whole benchmark
Comparing benchmark results across different machines without normalization
